A brief summary of the material facts claimed by: PLAINTFF: This is a products liability action arising pursuant to the Louisiana Product Liability Act (LPLA). Plaintiff claims that her daughter, Harmony Moller, died of sudden cardiac arrest due to the ingestion of OPMS kratom on February 6, 2023. -7-

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 313 Filed 03/11/26 Page 8 of 31 Plaintiff asserts that the OPMS product was manufactured by Defendants collectively as a single business enterprise engaged in the nationwide illegal importation and transportation of mitragynine spesiosa leaf, processing it into capsulated and powder form, packaging, and illegally distributing and selling the product in Louisiana and throughout the United States by placing it in the nationwide stream of commerce where it was purchased and consumed by the decedent. In the alternative, the core manufacturers under Louisiana law are Nuza, Calibre, Martian, and JOPEN. Plaintiff claims that the product was defective and unreasonably dangerous due to its design and inadequate warnings of potential cardiac death at the time it left Defendants’ control and which proximately caused the death of Harmony Moller. DEFENDANTS: This matter concerns Plaintiff Kathleen Moller’s “products liability claims under Louisiana’s Products Liability Act, La. R.S. 9:2800.51, et seq., asserting that the kratom product consumed by Harmony [her daughter] was unreasonably dangerous due to a failure to warn and a design defect.” Order and Reasons [Doc. 184] at 2; see also Third Amended Complaint (“TAC”) [Doc. 100]. O.P.M.S. Silver kratom is the sole product at issue in this lawsuit. The O.P.M.S. Silver product allegedly consumed by Harmony Moller is a pure kratom leaf powder that was sold lawfully in Louisiana at the time she allegedly purchased it from unknown third-party retailers. Defendants are not retailers and did not sell any product to Plaintiff. Defendants LP, CAG, RMH, Johnson Foods, FMK, PNW, and CC US have no involvement with or control over O.P.M.S. Silver kratom products. Defendants Peyton Palaio, Mark Jennings, David Gabbay, and Mark Reilly had no involvement with the O.P.M.S. Silver product outside of their formal managerial roles with the corporate defendants. -8-

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 313 Filed 03/11/26 Page 9 of 31 All parties agree that a sudden cardiac event caused Harmony’s death. It is undisputed that Ms. Moller had a coronary anomaly described as an “abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff.” The coroner ordered limited postmortem toxicology testing that confirmed the presence of at least two drugs (promethazine, which was not prescribed to Harmony, and diphenhydramine) and marijuana (delta-9 THC and delta-9 Carboxy THC), all of which are scientifically proven to cause cardiac arrhythmias through QT prolongation. The postmortem level of mitragynine, an alkaloid in kratom, was at an exceedingly low level—one that scientific literature has shown is safe and well-tolerated. Plaintiff’s entire case rests on the speculative leap that this low level of mitragynine, and not the combination of a serious heart defect and other potent drugs, was the cause of her daughter’s death. This speculation is compounded by the fact there is no direct evidence Ms. Moller even consumed Defendants’ O.P.M.S. Silver product before her death. In addition, in February 2023, there was no scientific or medical data to suggest that a low, well-tolerated level of mitragynine could cause a fatal cardiac event. And the O.P.M.S. Silver packaging contained a robust warning that explicitly instructed the user to consult a physician before use—a warning Harmony undisputedly ignored. Any additional warning would have been futile. 7. A single listing of all uncontested material facts. a. Harmony Moller died on February 6, 2023; b. A postmortem autopsy and a limited toxicology screen was performed; c. Mitragynine was detected in the decedent’s postmortem toxicology screens authorized by the St. Tammany Parish Coroner’s Office; d. At least two drugs (promethazine, which was not prescribed to Harmony Moller, and diphenhydramine) were detected in the decedent’s postmortem toxicology screens authorized by the St. Tammany Parish Coroner’s Office; e. Two unopened packages of OPMS kratom were found at decedent’s residence; -9-

Two alkaloids in kratom are mitragynine and 7-hydroxymitragynine, which interact with receptors in the brain. ggg. Kratom has been consumed for thousands of years in Southeast Asia. Kratom was traditionally used in Southeast Asia for fatigue and to improve stamina (by laborers), pain relief, and for opium withdrawal. hhh. Kratom is typically consumed as crushed leaves, powder, extracts, capsules, liquids, or brewed into tea. iii. In the U.S. and elsewhere, kratom is used to help with chronic pain, anxiety or depression, and opioid withdrawal or substitution. jjj. Unlike opioids, kratom does not produce respiratory depressant effects, nor carry opioid- like risks of death. kkk. The product at issue here consists only of ground leaves from the tree – there is no other ingredient. lll. These factual statements have been evaluated and verified as true by the Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”), the U.S. Assistant Secretary of Health, and the World Health Organization’s Expert Committee on Drug Dependence which conducted an initial review to determine if kratom warranted a full review as a potential path to international scheduling and determined that the evidence did not warrant such. mmm. Kratom is not an opioid or narcotic due to the nature of its botanical origin, its chemical structure, its known overall pharmacology, and the fact that it does not have the high abuse potential and national drug threat assessment necessary to meet statutory requirements for U.S. Controlled Substances Act (“CSA”) Scheduling or requirements for inclusion in the United Nations International Drug Control Treaties. nnn. Most people use kratom for health and well-being, including as a supplement to, or replacement for, caffeinated beverages and to self-manage depression, anxiety, pain, opioid and other drug withdrawal. -14-

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 313 Filed 03/11/26 Page 15 of 31 ooo. The vast majority of the evidence from which the foregoing facts were obtained was generated by independent researchers primarily supported by the National Institutes of Health (“NIH”) and NIDA. ppp. These studies have been published at an increasing rate year by year over the past decade in leading biomedical research institutions, including Johns Hopkins, University of Florida, the NIDA intramural program itself, and many others. qqq. Kratom is a legally marketed and sold in 43 states. rrr. Several of the states that placed kratom as a Schedule I drug in their Controlled Substances Act between 2014 to 2016 are presently in the process of replacing those laws with laws to ensure legal access. sss. Kratom is legally sold in the United States after Congress, the DEA, and the Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”)—the agency under which the FDA is organized— intensively investigated and deliberated about how to classify it. ttt. The Secretary of HHS and Commissioner of the FDA have both testified before Congress that it is in the public health interest to keep kratom available for purchase over the counter. They concluded that thousands of people would die from opioid overdoes if kratom was not made available as a substitute to opioids to the millions of people in the country who regularly purchase kratom. uuu. On August 21, 2014, the DEA requested that HHS conduct a medical and scientific evaluation of kratom to determine whether it should be recommended for scheduling as a controlled substance pursuant to the CSA. While HHS’s evaluation was ongoing, on August 31, 2016, the DEA announced its intent to temporarily add kratom to Schedule I of the CSA. In response, thousands of citizens submitted numerous formal comments providing compelling evidence and testimony that kratom is not harmful, but rather critical to healing, managing pain, and combating opiate and alcohol addiction. These comments explained that kratom is safer than prescription opioids and that, compared to opioids, deaths attributable to kratom overdose are essentially non-existent. vvv. U.S. Representatives Mark Pocan (D-WI) and Matt Salmon (R-AZ) sent a letter to DEA and the Office of Management and Budget—a letter that received bipartisan support and was signed by 50 members of Congress—against any ban. The letter noted that kratom is an internationally consumed herb and condemned the proposed ban as “hasty” because of known beneficial effects of kratom. The letter said that a ban would adversely affect consumer access to kratom’s known benefits and undermine innovative products that could be used to treat individuals suffering from addiction. www. A bipartisan group of U.S. Senators sent a generally similar letter to the DEA as the Representatives letter, making similar arguments about the adverse public health benefits of a Schedule I ban. The co-sponsors were Orrin G. Hatch (R-UT), Michael F. Bennet (D- -15-

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 313 Filed 03/11/26 Page 16 of 31 CO), Angus S. King, Jr. (I-ME), Mark Kirk (R-IL), Mike Lee (R-UT), Bernard Sanders (I- VT), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Mark R. Warner (D-VA), and Ron Wyden (D-OR). xxx. Less than two months later, on October 13, 2016, the DEA withdrew its intent to schedule kratom because of “numerous comments from the public.” The DEA stated that it was persuaded to take the highly unusual action of reversing itself because of the need to consider “comments offering their opinions regarding the pharmacological effects of these substances.” yyy. The DEA “requested that the FDA expedite its scientific and medical evaluation and scheduling recommendation for this substance, which DEA previously requested . . . .” The agency also set a December 1, 2016 deadline for additional comments and in fact received more than 23,000 comments during the 6-week comment period—most of which supported access to kratom. zzz. On October 1, 2017, HHS officials wrote a letter to the DEA recommending scheduling kratom. Once again, many individuals—both scientists and members of the public— submitted comments echoing the sentiment of the thousands of citizens who similarly opposed the ban when attempted in 2016. aaaa. For example, Dr. Andrew Kruegel, a Columbia University Professor of Chemistry studying kratom, stated: “I have major concerns about just pulling the rug out from under tens of thousands of people who are using this to support their health, especially in the case of people who are using it to stay off of more dangerous opioids.” bbbb. Researchers also expressed that scheduling kratom would make it more difficult to study kratom, because any clinical study would require the DEA’s permission. cccc. In August 2018 the Assistant Secretary of Health, Dr. Brett Giroir charged with FDA scheduling recommendations to DEA, withdrew FDA’s 2017 scheduling recommendation to the DEA. In the formal scheduling recission letter, he stated that the “recission is based on many factors, in part on new data, and in part on the relative lack of evidence, combined with an unknown and potentially substantial risk to public health if these chemicals were scheduled at this time.” As a result, the DEA ceased its scheduling efforts. This is the only time in United States’ history that the DEA has withdrawn a proposed scheduling. dddd.
